title: Fruited Sours and Smoothie Sours | Craft Beer School
desc: How fruited sours and thick smoothie sours are made, what lactose and purée do to the glass and the risks for brewers.
teaser: Some sours taste like fruit juice. Some pour like a milkshake. Here is what is going on in both.
standfirst: Fruited sours have become one of the most recognisable craft beer styles. Smoothie sours have pushed the idea to its limit. Here is how both are made, what to expect in the glass and why brewers treat them with care.
sections: A sour base with a lot of fruit

A fruited sour starts as a light, tart beer, usually kettle soured to a pH around 3.2 to 3.6. After fermentation the brewer adds fruit, often as purée because it is easier to handle than whole fruit. The yeast ferments some of the fruit sugar, which dries the beer out a little and lifts the fruit aroma.

The amount varies enormously. A lightly fruited sour might use a few tens of grams per litre. Heavily fruited versions can carry several hundred grams per litre, enough that the beer looks and tastes more like fruit than beer. Our guide to adding fruit to beer covers the handling side.
What makes a sour a smoothie sour

A smoothie sour takes the fruited sour and makes it thick. Brewers add large amounts of purée, often with lactose, a milk sugar that brewing yeast cannot ferment. Lactose stays in the beer as sweetness and body. Some recipes also add oats, vanilla or marshmallow-like flavours to push the dessert effect further.

The result can be opaque, almost spoonable and far sweeter than any traditional sour. Brewers sometimes describe them by their purée content rather than their acidity. Anyone with a dairy allergy or lactose intolerance should check the label before ordering, since the lactose is not obvious from the name. Our page on lactose in beer explains why it stays behind.
Why acid and sugar need each other

The appeal of these beers is balance. Acidity on its own can feel harsh. Sweetness on its own can feel cloying. Put them together and the acidity keeps the sweetness lively, much like a good mango lassi with a pinch of salt or an aam panna made with raw mango.

When that balance slips, the beer fails. Too little acid and a smoothie sour tastes like a thin fruit juice. Too much and the sugar cannot rescue it. Taste a few side by side and you will notice that the best ones still finish with enough tartness to make you want another sip.
The packaging risk brewers worry about

Fruit sugar keeps fermenting if live yeast is present. A can sealed with unfermented fruit sugar inside can build pressure over days or weeks, especially if it is stored warm. In bad cases cans bulge or burst.

Breweries manage this in a few ways: letting the fruit ferment out fully before packaging, pasteurising the finished beer, or keeping it cold from tank to fridge. For Indian distribution, where summer storage can sit above 35 °C, cold chain discipline matters. If a fruited sour can looks domed at the top or bottom, do not open it near your face. Return it.
Indian fruit is a gift for this style

Brewers here have fruit that the rest of the world pays a premium for. Alphonso and other mangoes, jamun, guava, passion fruit, kokum, pineapple and litchi all appear in Indian fruited beers. Each brings its own acidity and aroma. Kokum adds tartness and a deep pink colour. Jamun brings tannin and a purple tint. Guava has a perfume that survives fermentation well.

Seasonality matters. A beer made with fresh pulp during mango season can taste very different from one made with frozen purée later in the year. That variation is part of the charm, as long as the brewery is honest about it.
Fruit in sour beer is an old idea

The modern fruited sour feels new, but brewers in Belgium have added fruit to sour beer for a long time. Kriek is lambic aged on sour cherries. Framboise uses raspberries. In both, the fruit sits in the beer for months, the wild yeast ferments almost all of its sugar and what remains is dry, tart and deeply fruity.

The difference today is speed and sweetness. A traditional kriek might spend a year or more in oak. A modern fruited kettle sour can go from brew day to can in two or three weeks, with fruit added late so more of its fresh aroma survives. Smoothie sours go further by keeping sugar in the beer on purpose.

Neither approach is wrong. They are different drinks for different moments. A dry kriek suits a slow evening. A bright mango sour suits a hot afternoon. Knowing which one you are holding stops you judging one by the other's standards.
How to taste them without getting fooled by sugar

Sweetness hides a lot. A smoothie sour can mask acetic notes, solvent-like alcohol or stale fruit behind its sugar. Trained tasters learn to look past the first sweet impression and judge the finish, the aroma and the acidity separately. That discipline takes practice with reference samples.

Try this: pour a fruited sour and a smoothie sour made with the same fruit, ideally from the same brewery. Taste each twice, once straight away and once after it has warmed for ten minutes. Write down how the sweetness, sourness and fruit aroma change. Warm beer is honest beer.
faqs: Many do. Lactose is a milk sugar commonly added for sweetness and body, so check the label if you avoid dairy.
How much fruit goes into a fruited sour?
It varies from a few tens of grams per litre in lightly fruited beers to several hundred grams per litre in the heaviest versions.
Why do some fruited sour cans bulge?
Leftover fruit sugar can keep fermenting in the can if live yeast is present, building pressure. A bulging can should be returned unopened.
Are fruited sours a traditional style?
Fruit in sour beer is old, as Belgian kriek and framboise show. The heavily fruited and smoothie versions are a recent craft development.
